newsitem.title: UK: French Socialists could delay EMU -DRI/McGraw-Hill.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists could delay EMU -DRI/McGraw-Hill.

text.p: The domestic policies of France's new Socialist government mean European economic and monetary union (EMU) is highly unlikely to start on time, analysts at economic consultants DRI/McGraw-Hill, said on Tuesday.

DRI/McGraw-Hill analysts noted that Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's Socialists' campaign against any further measures to cut French public deficit to the three percent of GDP required by the Maastricht criteria would leave the deficit at 3.4 percent or more for 1997.
They also said Jospin's insistence on the inclusion in EMU of Italy and Britain, if it wants to participate, would provide obstacles to EMU going ahead on schedule in 1999.

"With the French deficit well above the Maastricht criteria, EMU in 1999 with France and without Italy is highly unlikely and Jospin's position over Italy virtually rules out any attempts by the German government to successfully negotiate a core EMU, excluding Italy, to start on time."
They said they expected Germany to face an ultimatum to accept EMU with Italy on time or agree to a delay at the final negotiations next spring.

DRI/McGraw-Hill said there was a 60 percent chance of EMU including Italy going ahead on time or with a delay of 12 months, a 15 percent chance of EMU with a core group of economies excluding Italy going ahead on time or up to 12 months delayed and a 25 percent chance of EMU delayed beyond the year 2000, DRI/McGraw-Hill said.

Analysts at the consultancy, a division of Standard and Poor's, predicted Germany would suffer from next year's negotiations, experiencing downward pressure on the mark and an acceleration to the convergence between Italian and German bond yields.
